title: Stop Fighting. Start Moving.
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer writes to leaders about conflict, starting from the observation that other people are what make leading hard. Within her Leadership Connection Model she names only three leadership skills, communication, conscious choice and conflict resolution, and argues that most people's unresolved relationship with the third one quietly prevents them from offering their leadership at all. Her central move is to reframe what a conflict actually is. Rather than two opposing sides competing to win, she describes two people who each care about an outcome, one of whom has come to believe the other holds control over whether that outcome is possible. That belief is where attention shifts from the thing being built to the person apparently blocking it, and where energy starts going into defeating an opponent instead. The piece's governing image is two people yelling across a street: as long as winning the argument is the objective, both stay put, busy and loud and immobile, and the only way forward is to turn and start walking toward the original destination. Schafer is careful to carve out conflicts that demand direct engagement, where harm must be named and accountability enforced, so the argument is not for avoidance but for refusing to let opposition set your direction.
points: Schafer reduces leadership to three skills in her Leadership Connection Model, communication, conscious choice and conflict resolution, and argues the third is what most often stops people from leading at all.
Her reframe is that conflict is rarely two opposing sides but two people who each want an outcome, one of whom has begun to believe the other controls whether they can have it.
The street-yelling image carries the argument: facing your opponent and refuting each point keeps you passionate, loud and stationary, while turning and walking is conscious choice in practice.
She names the diagnostic question directly, asking where you were trying to go before this person became the focus of your attention.
Schafer explicitly exempts conflicts that require direct engagement, where harm must be named and people held accountable, so the piece is not a case for avoidance.
quotes: In the Leadership Connection Model, I identify only three leadership skills: communication, conscious choice and conflict resolution.
Today, I want to focus on conflict resolution because our relationship with it prevents far too many people from fully offering their leadership.
They each have a desired outcome. And somewhere along the way, at least one begins to believe the other person has control over whether they can have what they want.
Our attention shifts away from what we wanted to create and toward the person we believe is standing in the way.
Soon, tremendous energy is being spent defeating the other side while the thing we originally cared about sits somewhere off in the distance.
People become so focused on the fight that winning the fight begins to replace achieving the desired outcome.
There are, of course, conflicts that require direct engagement. Harm needs to be named. Boundaries need to be established. People need to be held accountable.
This is very different from pretending opposition does not exist. It is refusing to hand opposition control of our direction.
